title: The Story of Two Sisters Who Were Jealous of Their Younger Sister
paragraphs: Once upon a time Persia was ruled by a Sultan named Kosrouschah. Since boyhood he had loved to put on a disguise and go looking for adventures all over the city, with one of his officers dressed up beside him. As soon as his father was buried and the ceremonies of his accession were over, the young man hurried to take off his robes of state. He called his vizier to get ready in the same way, and the two slipped out in the plain clothes of ordinary citizens into the lesser known streets of the capital.

As he walked down a lonely street, the Sultan heard women’s voices arguing loudly. He peeped through a crack in a door and saw three sisters sitting on a sofa in a large hall, talking in a lively, earnest way. From the few words that reached him, he gathered that each was describing the kind of man she wanted to marry.

“I ask for nothing better,” cried the eldest, “than the Sultan’s baker for a husband. Think of eating as much as you liked of that delicious bread, baked for his Highness alone! Let’s see if your wish is as good as mine.”

“I,” answered the second sister, “would be quite happy with the Sultan’s head cook. Think of the delicate stews I would feast on! And since I’m sure the Sultan’s bread is used all through the palace, I would get that as well. You see, dear sister, my taste is as good as yours.”

Now it was the youngest sister’s turn. She was by far the most beautiful of the three, and she had more sense than the other two as well. “As for me,” she said, “I would aim higher. If we are going to wish for husbands, nothing less than the Sultan himself will do for me.”

The Sultan was so amused by what he had overheard that he decided to grant their wishes. He turned to the grand vizier, told him to take note of the house, and ordered him to bring the ladies into his presence the next morning.

The grand vizier carried out his orders. He barely gave the sisters time to change their clothes before telling them to follow him to the palace. There they were presented one by one, and after they had bowed before the Sultan, he put a sudden question to them.
“Tell me, do you remember what you wished for last night, when you were making merry? Don’t be afraid, and tell me the truth.”

These unexpected words threw the sisters into great confusion. They lowered their eyes, and the youngest’s blushes did not fail to touch the Sultan’s heart. All three stayed silent, so he went on quickly: “Don’t be afraid. I have no wish to hurt you, and let me tell you at once that I know what each of you wished for. You,” he said, turning to the youngest, “who wanted me for a husband, will have your wish this very day. And you,” he added, speaking to the other two, “will be married at the same moment to my baker and my chief cook.”

When the Sultan had finished, the three sisters threw themselves at his feet. The youngest stammered, “Oh, sire, since you know my foolish words, please believe they were said only as a joke. I am unworthy of the honor you mean to do me, and I can only beg pardon for my boldness.”
The other sisters tried to excuse themselves too, but the Sultan would not listen.
“No, no,” he said, “my mind is made up. Your wishes will be granted.”

So all three weddings were held that same day, but with a great difference. The youngest sister’s was marked by all the magnificence customary at the marriage of the Shah of Persia, while the celebrations for the Sultan’s baker and his chief cook were only what suited their stations.

This was natural enough, but it displeased the elder sisters greatly. They were seized by a fit of jealousy that in the end brought much trouble and pain to several people. The first chance they had to speak to each other was several days later, at a public bath, and they made no attempt to hide their feelings.
“Can you understand what the Sultan saw in that little cat,” said one to the other, “to be so taken with her?”
“He must be quite blind,” answered the chief cook’s wife. “And so what if she looks a little younger than we do? That hardly matters. You would have made a far better Sultana than she.”

“Oh, I say nothing of myself,” replied the elder, “and if the Sultan had chosen you, that would have been fine. But it really grieves me that he picked a wretched little creature like that. Still, I will have my revenge on her somehow, and I beg you to help me, and to tell me anything you can think of that is likely to humiliate her.”

To carry out their wicked scheme, the two sisters met constantly to talk over their ideas, all the while acting as friendly as ever toward the Sultana, who went on treating them kindly. For a long time they could think of no plan that seemed to have the slightest chance of working. But at last the Sultana was expecting a child, and that gave them the opening they had been hoping for.

They asked the Sultan if they might move into the palace for a few weeks, and from then on they never left their sister’s side, day or night. When a baby boy, as beautiful as the sun, was finally born, they put him in a cradle and carried it down to a canal that ran through the palace grounds. They set it adrift and left it to its fate. Then they told the Sultan that the Sultana had given birth to a puppy, not the son he had longed for so dearly. The news threw the Sultan into such a rage and such grief that the grand vizier had great trouble saving the Sultana from his anger.
The cradle, meanwhile, kept floating calmly along the canal. At the edge of the royal gardens the intendant spotted it, one of the highest and most respected officials in the kingdom.
“Go and fetch that cradle out for me,” he told a gardener who was working nearby.
The gardener did as he was told and soon had the cradle in the intendant’s hands.

The intendant was amazed. He had taken the cradle for an empty one, but there was a baby inside, and even at that age the child showed signs of great beauty. He and his wife had been married some years without having children, and it struck him at once that here was a child he could take in and raise as his own. He told the gardener to pick up the cradle and follow, and set off for home.

“Wife,” he called as he came into the room, “heaven has refused us children, but it has sent us this one instead. Find a nurse, and I will do whatever is needed to acknowledge him publicly as our son.”
His wife took the baby gladly. The intendant could see perfectly well that the child must have come from the royal palace, but he did not think it was his place to look into the mystery any further.

The next year a second prince was born and set adrift, and the baby was lucky: the intendant of the gardens again happened to be walking beside the canal, and he took this child home just as he had the first.

The second time, the Sultan was even angrier than the first, and when the same strange thing happened again in the third year, he could hold back no longer. To the great delight of the jealous sisters, he ordered the Sultana to be put to death. But she was so loved at court that the grand vizier and the courtiers, though they risked the same fate, threw themselves at the Sultan’s feet and begged him not to inflict so cruel a punishment for something that, after all, was not her fault.
“Let her live,” the grand vizier pleaded, “and send her away from you for the rest of her life. That alone will be punishment enough.”

The Sultan’s first fury had passed, and he had himself under control again. “Then let her live,” he said, “since you care so much about it. But I will spare her only on one condition, one that will make her pray for death every day. Have a box built for her by the door of the main mosque, and keep its window always open. She will sit there in the coarsest clothes, and every Muslim who goes into the mosque will spit in her face as he passes. Anyone who refuses will suffer the same punishment himself. Vizier, you will see that my orders are carried out.”

The grand vizier saw there was no point in arguing further. The sisters, full of triumph, watched the box being built and then listened to the crowd jeering at the helpless Sultana sitting inside. But the poor lady carried herself with such dignity and gentleness that before long she had won the sympathy of the better people in the crowd.

But now we must go back to the third baby, a princess this time. Like her brothers, she was found by the intendant of the gardens, and he and his wife took her in. All three children were raised with the greatest care and tenderness.

As the children grew, their beauty and noble bearing showed more and more, and their manners had all the grace and ease of people of high birth. Their foster father had named the princes Bahman and Perviz, after two of the ancient kings of Persia, and the princess he called Parizade, which means child of the genies.

The intendant took care to bring them up in a way that suited their true rank, and before long he hired a tutor to teach the young princes to read and write. The princess was determined not to be left behind. She was so eager to learn alongside her brothers that the intendant agreed to let her join their lessons, and it was not long before she knew as much as they did.

From then on they studied everything together. They had the best teachers for the arts, geography, poetry, history and science, and even for sciences that few people learn. Every subject came so easily to them that their teachers were amazed at how fast they advanced. The princess loved music and could sing and play every kind of instrument. She could also ride and drive a carriage as well as her brothers, shoot with a bow and arrow, and throw a javelin as skillfully as they did, and sometimes better.

To give these talents room to show themselves, the intendant decided that his foster children should no longer be shut up within the narrow bounds of the palace gardens, where he had always lived. He bought a splendid country house a few miles from the capital, with an immense park around it. He filled the park with wild animals of many kinds, so that the princes and the princess could hunt as much as they liked.

When all was ready, the intendant threw himself at the Sultan’s feet. He spoke of his age and his long years of service and begged his Highness’s permission to give up his post. The Sultan granted it in a few kind words and then asked what reward he could give his faithful servant. The intendant said he wanted nothing but the continued favor of his Highness. He prostrated himself once more and left the Sultan’s presence.

Five or six months went by in the pleasures of country life, and then death struck the intendant so suddenly that he had no time to tell his adopted children the secret of their birth. His wife had died long before, so it seemed the princes and the princess would never learn that they had been born to a higher station than the one they now held. They grieved deeply for their father, and they went on living quietly in their new home, with no wish to leave it for the amusements and intrigues of the court.

One day the princes went out hunting as usual, but their sister stayed behind in her apartments. While they were away, an old Muslim woman, a devotee, came to the door and asked to come in, because it was the hour of prayer. The princess immediately sent word that the old woman should be taken to the private prayer room in the grounds, and that when she had finished praying she should be shown around the house and gardens and then brought to her.

The old woman was very pious, but she was far from indifferent to the magnificence around her, and she seemed to understand it as well as admire it. When she had seen everything, the servants led her to the princess, who was sitting in a room more splendid than all the rest.

“Good woman,” said the princess, pointing to a sofa, “come and sit next to me. I am delighted to have the chance to talk for a few moments with such a holy person.” The old woman protested that this was too great an honor, but the princess would not listen. She insisted that her guest take the best seat, and, thinking she must be tired, ordered refreshments.
While the old woman ate, the princess asked her many questions about how she lived and what devotions she practiced. Then she asked what she thought of the house, now that she had seen it all.

“Madam,” answered the pilgrim, “you would have to be very hard to please to find fault with it. It is beautiful, comfortable and well kept, and nothing could be lovelier than the garden. But since you ask me, I have to admit that it lacks three things to make it truly perfect.”
“And what are they?” cried the princess. “Just tell me, and I will lose no time in getting them.”

“The three things, madam,” the old woman answered, “are these. First, the Talking Bird, whose voice calls every other singing bird to come and sing along with it. Second, the Singing Tree, where every leaf is a song and the singing never stops. And last, the Golden Water. You need only pour a single drop of it into a basin, and it shoots up into a fountain that never runs dry, while the basin never overflows.”
“How can I ever thank you,” cried the princess, “for telling me about such treasures! But please be kinder still, and tell me where I can find them.”

“Madam,” said the pilgrim, “I would be repaying your hospitality badly if I refused to answer. The three things I spoke of are all in one place, on the edge of this kingdom, toward India. Your messenger only has to follow the road that passes your house for twenty days. At the end of that time he should ask the first person he meets for the Talking Bird, the Singing Tree and the Golden Water.” Then she got up, said goodbye to the princess and went on her way.

The old woman left so suddenly that Princess Parizade did not realize until she was truly gone that the directions were hardly clear enough for a search to succeed. She was still thinking about it, and how wonderful it would be to own such rarities, when her brothers the princes came back from the hunt.
“What is wrong, sister?” asked Prince Bahman. “Why are you so serious? Are you ill? Or has something happened?”
Princess Parizade did not answer right away. After a while she looked up and said that nothing was wrong.

“But there must be something,” Prince Bahman insisted, “because you have changed so much in the short time we have been gone. Please hide nothing from us, unless you want us to believe that the trust we have always had in each other is over.”

“When I said it was nothing,” said the princess, moved by his words, “I meant it was nothing that concerns you, though I admit it matters a good deal to me. Like me, you have always thought this house our father built for us was perfect in every way. But only today I learned that three things are still missing from it. They are the Talking Bird, the Singing Tree and the Golden Water.” After describing the special qualities of each, the princess went on: “It was a devout Muslim woman who told me all this, and where they might be found. Perhaps you will think the house is beautiful enough as it is and that we can do without them, but I cannot agree, and I will not be content until I have them. So advise me, please, whom I should send on this errand.”

“Dear sister,” answered Prince Bahman, “the fact that you care about this is reason enough, even if we had no interest in it ourselves. But we both feel as you do, and as the elder, I claim the right to make the first attempt, if you will tell me where to go and what to do.”

Prince Perviz first objected that his brother should not be allowed to risk danger, since he was the head of the family. But Prince Bahman would hear none of it, and he went off to prepare for his journey.

Early the next morning Prince Bahman got up, said goodbye to his brother and sister, and mounted his horse. But just as he was about to touch the horse with his whip, a cry from the princess stopped him.

“Oh, perhaps you will never come back after all. You never know what might happen. Please give it up, because I would a thousand times rather lose the Talking Bird, the Singing Tree and the Golden Water than have you run into danger.”

“Dear sister,” the prince answered, “accidents only happen to unlucky people, and I hope I am not one of them. But since nothing is certain, I promise to be very careful. Take this knife,” he went on, handing her one that hung in its sheath from his belt, “and every so often, pull it out and look at it. As long as the blade stays as bright and clean as it is today, you will know I am alive. But if it is spotted with blood, that will be a sign that I am dead, and then you may weep for me.”

With that, Prince Bahman said goodbye to them once more and set off down the high road, well mounted and fully armed. For twenty days he rode straight ahead, turning neither right nor left, until he was nearing the borders of Persia. Sitting under a tree beside the road he saw a hideous old man with a long white mustache and a beard that nearly reached his feet. His nails had grown enormously long, and on his head he wore a huge hat that served him as an umbrella.

Prince Bahman remembered the old woman’s directions and had been watching for someone since sunrise. He knew at once that the old man was a dervish. He got down from his horse and bowed low before the holy man, greeting him with these words: “Father, may your days be long in the land, and may all your wishes come true!”

The dervish tried his best to answer, but his mustache was so thick that his words could hardly be understood. The prince saw the problem, took a pair of scissors from his saddle pockets, and asked permission to cut off some of the mustache, since he had a very important question for the dervish. The dervish signed that he could do as he liked. When a few inches of hair and beard had been trimmed all around, the prince told the holy man he would hardly believe how much younger he looked. The dervish smiled at the compliment and thanked him for what he had done.
“Let me show my gratitude,” he said, “for making me more comfortable, by asking what I can do for you.”

“Kind dervish,” answered Prince Bahman, “I have come a long way looking for the Talking Bird, the Singing Tree and the Golden Water. I know they lie somewhere in this region, but I don’t know exactly where. Please tell me, if you can, so that my journey won’t have been for nothing.” As he spoke, the prince saw the dervish’s face change, and the old man said nothing for some time.
“My lord,” he said at last, “I do know the road you’re asking about. But I’ve grown fond of you, and you’ve been so kind to me, that I hate to point it out.”
“Why not?” asked the prince. “What’s the danger?”

“The greatest danger there is,” the dervish answered. “Other men as brave as you have ridden down that road and asked me the same thing. I did all I could to talk them out of it too, but it was no use. Not one of them would listen, and not one of them ever came back. Take my warning while there is still time, and go no further.”
“I’m grateful for your concern, and for your advice,” said Prince Bahman, “though I can’t follow it. But what danger could there be in this adventure that courage and a good sword can’t face?”
“And what if your enemies can’t be seen?” said the dervish. “What then?”
“Nothing will ever make me give it up,” the prince replied, “and for the last time I ask you to tell me where I am to go.”

Seeing that the prince had made up his mind, the dervish took a ball out of a bag beside him and held it out. “If it has to be,” he said with a sigh, “take this. Once you are on your horse, throw the ball ahead of you. It will roll until it reaches the foot of a mountain, and when it stops, you stop too. Then drop the reins on your horse’s neck, since he won’t wander off, and get down. On both sides you will see huge heaps of big black stones, and you will hear a crowd of voices jeering at you. Pay them no attention, and above all, never turn your head. If you do, you will turn at once into a black stone like the others. Those stones are really men like you, who set out on this same quest and failed, as I’m afraid you may fail too. If you avoid this trap and reach the top of the mountain, you will find the Talking Bird in a splendid cage, and you can ask him where to look for the Singing Tree and the Golden Water. That is all I have to tell you. You know what you must do and what you must avoid. But if you are wise, you will think no more of it and go back the way you came.”
The prince smiled and shook his head. He thanked the dervish again, leapt onto his horse and threw the ball ahead of him.

The ball rolled down the road so fast that Prince Bahman could hardly keep up, and it never slowed until it reached the foot of the mountain. There it stopped dead. The prince got down at once and dropped the reins on his horse’s neck. He stood a moment looking at the masses of black stones that covered the mountainside, and then he started up with firm resolve. He had barely taken four steps when he heard voices all around him, though there was no living creature in sight.

“Who is this fool?” some cried. “Stop him now!” “Kill him!” others shrieked. “Help! Thieves! Murderers! Help! Help!” “Oh, leave him alone,” sneered another voice, and this was the hardest to bear. “He’s such a handsome young man. I’m sure the bird and the cage have been saved for him.”

At first the prince ignored the uproar and kept climbing. Unfortunately, instead of quieting the voices, this seemed only to enrage them, and they rose to a still wilder fury, ahead of him as well as behind. After a while he became confused, his knees began to shake, and as he felt himself about to fall, he forgot the dervish’s advice completely. He turned to run down the mountain, and in that instant he became a black stone.

As you can imagine, Prince Perviz and his sister were extremely anxious all this while, and they looked at the magic knife many times a day, not just once. Until then the blade had stayed bright and clean, but at the fatal hour when Prince Bahman and his horse were turned into black stones, large drops of blood appeared on it. “Oh, my dear brother!” cried the princess in horror, flinging the knife away. “I will never see you again, and I am the one who killed you. What a fool I was to listen to that temptress, who probably wasn’t telling the truth. What do the Talking Bird and the Singing Tree matter to me compared with you, however passionately I long for them!”
Prince Perviz grieved for his brother just as much as Princess Parizade did, but he didn’t waste his time on pointless mourning.

“Sister,” he said, “why would you think the old woman was lying to you about these treasures? And what would she have gained by it? No, our brother must have died through some accident, or because he wasn’t careful enough. Tomorrow I will set out on the same quest.”

The princess was terrified of losing her only remaining brother and begged him to give up the plan, but he stood firm. Before leaving, however, he gave her a string of a hundred pearls and said, “While I’m away, count these beads every day for me. But if you find that they stick and won’t slide one after another, you’ll know that my brother’s fate has befallen me. Still, let us hope for better luck.”

Then he left, and on the twentieth day of his journey he met the dervish at the very spot where Prince Bahman had met him. He began asking where the Talking Bird, the Singing Tree and the Golden Water could be found. As with his brother, the dervish tried to talk him out of it, and even told him that only a few weeks earlier a young man who looked very much like him had passed that way and never returned.
“Holy dervish,” answered Prince Perviz, “that was my elder brother. He is dead now, though I can’t say how he died.”

“He has been turned into a black stone,” the dervish answered, “like everyone else who has gone on this errand, and you will become one too unless you follow my directions more carefully.” Then he ordered the prince, as he valued his life, to pay no attention to the voices that would chase him up the mountain. He handed him a ball from the bag, which still seemed half full, and sent him on his way.

When Prince Perviz reached the foot of the mountain, he jumped off his horse and stopped for a moment to recall the dervish’s instructions. Then he marched boldly forward. But he had hardly gone five or six paces when a man’s voice, right beside his ear, startled him: “Stop, you reckless fool, and let me punish your insolence!” This insult drove the dervish’s advice clean out of the prince’s head. He drew his sword and spun around to take revenge, but before he had even understood that nobody was there, he and his horse had become two black stones.

Not one morning went by after Prince Perviz rode off without Princess Parizade counting her beads, and at night she even wore them around her neck, so that if she woke she could check at once that her brother was safe. She was running them through her fingers at the very moment the prince fell victim to his impatience, and her heart sank when the first pearl stayed stuck in place. But she had long ago decided what she would do in that case, and the next morning the princess dressed as a man and set out for the mountain.

She had been used to riding since childhood, so she covered as many miles each day as her brothers had, and again it was on the twentieth day that she reached the place where the dervish sat. “Good dervish,” she said politely, “may I rest beside you for a few moments? And would you be kind enough to tell me whether you have ever heard of a Talking Bird, a Singing Tree and some Golden Water, which are said to be somewhere near here?”
“Madam,” said the dervish, “for your voice gives you away in spite of your man’s clothes, I would be proud to help you in any way I can. But may I ask why you want to know?”
“Good dervish,” the princess answered, “I have heard such glowing accounts of these three things that I can’t rest until I own them.”

“Madam,” said the dervish, “they are far lovelier than any account of them. But you seem to know nothing of the difficulties in your way, or you would hardly have taken on such an adventure. Please give it up and go home, and don’t ask me to help you to a cruel death.”

“Holy father,” the princess answered, “I have come a long way, and I would be in despair if I turned back without getting what I came for. You mention difficulties. Please tell me what they are, so that I can find out whether I can overcome them or whether they are beyond my strength.”

So the dervish told his story again. This time he stressed even more strongly the shouting of the voices, the horror of the black stones that had once been living men, and the difficulty of climbing the mountain. He also pointed out that the key to success was never to look back until you had the cage in your hands.

“As I understand it,” said the princess, “the first thing is to ignore the din of the voices that follow you until you reach the cage, and the second is never to look back. I believe I have enough self-control to keep my eyes straight ahead. But the voices might well frighten me, as they have frightened even the boldest men, so I will plug my ears with cotton. They can make all the noise they like, and I will hear nothing.”
“Madam,” cried the dervish, “of all the people who have asked me the way to the mountain, you are the first to think of such a way to escape the danger! You may succeed, but the risk is still great.”
“Good dervish,” the princess answered, “I feel in my heart that I will succeed. All I need now is for you to tell me which way to go.”
Then the dervish said there was no point in saying more, and he gave her the ball, which she threw ahead of her.

As soon as she arrived at the mountain, the princess plugged her ears with cotton. Then she chose the best route and began to climb. Despite the cotton, a few echoes of the voices reached her, but they didn’t bother her. In fact, though they grew louder and more insulting the higher she climbed, the princess only laughed and told herself that a few rough words would certainly not stand between her and her goal. At last she saw the cage and the bird in the distance. His voice joined the others in a thunderous roar: “Go back, go back! Don’t you dare come near me!”

When she saw the bird, the princess quickened her pace. Without letting the noise trouble her, which by now was deafening, she walked straight up to the cage and seized it. “Now, bird, I have you,” she said, “and I will make sure you don’t escape.” As she spoke, she pulled the cotton out of her ears, since she no longer needed it.

“Brave lady,” the bird answered, “don’t blame me for joining my voice to those who did their best to protect my freedom. Even shut in a cage I was content with my lot. But if I must be a slave, I couldn’t wish for a nobler mistress than one who has shown such steadfastness, and from this moment I swear to serve you faithfully. Some day you will put me to the test, for I know who you are better than you know yourself. For now, tell me what I can do for you, and I will obey.”

“Bird,” said the princess, who felt a joy that seemed strange even to her, when she thought that the bird had cost her the lives of both her brothers, “bird, let me first thank you for your goodwill. Then tell me, please, where I can find the Golden Water.”

The bird described the place, which was not far away, and the princess filled a small silver flask that she had brought for the purpose. Then she went back to the cage and said, “Bird, there is one more thing. Where will I find the Singing Tree?”

“Behind you, in that wood,” the bird replied. The princess walked through the wood until the sound of the sweetest voices told her she had found what she was looking for. But the tree was tall and strong, and there was no hope of pulling it up by the roots.
“You don’t need to,” said the bird, when she came back to ask his advice. “Break off a twig and plant it in your garden. It will take root and grow into a magnificent tree.”

Now Princess Parizade held in her hands the three wonders the old woman had promised her. She said to the bird, “That is not enough. It was because of you that my brothers became black stones. I can’t tell them apart from all the others, but you must know which they are, so please point them out to me, for I want to take them away.”

For some reason the princess couldn’t guess, these words seemed to displease the bird, and he made no answer. The princess waited a moment and then went on in a stern voice, “Have you forgotten that you yourself said you are my slave and will do as I command, and also that your life is in my power?”

“No, I haven’t forgotten,” said the bird, “but what you ask is very hard. Still, I will do my best. If you look around,” he went on, “you will see a pitcher standing nearby. Take it, and as you go down the mountain, sprinkle a little of the water in it over every black stone, and you will soon find your two brothers.”

Princess Parizade took the pitcher. Carrying the cage, the twig and the flask as well, she went back down the mountainside. She stopped at every black stone and sprinkled it with water, and the moment the water touched it, the stone turned into a man. When she suddenly saw her brothers in front of her, her delight was mixed with astonishment.
“Why, what are you doing here?” she cried.
“We have been asleep,” they said.

“Yes,” answered the princess, “but if I hadn’t come, you would probably have slept until the Day of Judgment. Have you forgotten why you came here? You came looking for the Talking Bird, the Singing Tree and the Golden Water, and for the black stones piled along the road. Look around you and see whether a single one is left. These gentlemen, you yourselves and all your horses had been turned into those stones, and I set you free by sprinkling you with water from this pitcher. I couldn’t go home without you, even with the prizes I had set my heart on, so I made the Talking Bird tell me how to break the spell.”

When Prince Bahman and Prince Perviz heard this, they realized how much they owed their sister. The knights standing nearby declared themselves her slaves, ready to do whatever she wished. The princess thanked them for their courtesy, but she explained that she wanted no company except her brothers, and that everyone else was free to go wherever they liked.

With that, the princess got on her horse. She would not even let Prince Bahman carry the cage with the Talking Bird; she gave him the branch of the Singing Tree to hold instead, and Prince Perviz looked after the flask of Golden Water.
Then they rode off, with the knights and gentlemen behind them, who had begged to be allowed to escort them.

The party had meant to stop and tell the dervish about their adventures, but to their sorrow they found him dead. Whether he died of old age, or because he felt his work was finished, they never found out.

As they went on their way, their company shrank a little more each day, because the knights left one by one for their own homes. In the end only the brothers and their sister pulled up at the palace gate.

The princess carried the cage straight into the garden, and as soon as the bird began to sing, nightingales, larks, thrushes, finches and every other kind of bird joined in with a chorus. She planted the branch in a corner near the house, and within a few days it had grown into a big tree. The Golden Water was poured into a large marble basin built especially for it, where it swelled and bubbled and then shot up into the air as a fountain twenty feet high.
News of these wonders soon spread, and people came from far and wide to see and admire them.

After a few days Prince Bahman and Prince Perviz went back to their usual routine, spending most of their time hunting. One day the Sultan of Persia happened to be hunting in the same area. The young men heard the noise of his hunt coming closer and prepared to withdraw so as not to spoil his sport, but by bad luck they turned onto the very path the Sultan was riding down. They jumped off their horses and bowed to the ground. The Sultan, curious to see their faces, ordered them to get up.
The princes rose respectfully but without any awkwardness. The Sultan looked at them for a few moments in silence, then asked who they were and where they lived.

“Sire,” answered Prince Bahman, “we are the sons of Your Highness’s late superintendent of gardens. We live in a house he built shortly before he died, and we are waiting for a chance to serve Your Highness.”
“You seem to enjoy hunting,” said the Sultan.
“Sire,” answered Prince Bahman, “it is what we usually do for exercise, and no man should neglect it if he means to honor the ancient customs of the kingdom and bear arms.”
The Sultan was delighted with this answer. “In that case,” he said at once, “I’ll gladly watch you. Come, pick what sort of animals you’d like to hunt.”

The princes leaped onto their horses and followed the Sultan at a short distance. They hadn’t gone far when a number of wild animals appeared all at once. Prince Bahman set off after a lion and Prince Perviz after a bear. Both threw their javelins so skillfully that as soon as they came within range, the lion and the bear dropped, run clean through. Then Prince Perviz went after a lion and Prince Bahman after a bear, and within minutes those two lay dead as well. They were getting ready for a third attack when the Sultan stepped in. He sent one of his officials to call them back and said with a smile, “If I let you carry on, there will soon be no animals left to hunt. Besides, your courage and your manners have won my heart so completely that I won’t let you risk yourselves any more. I’m convinced that one day I’ll find you useful as well as pleasant company.”
Then he warmly invited them to stay with him for good. They thanked him many times for the honor, but begged to be excused and allowed to stay at home.

The Sultan was not used to having his offers turned down, and he asked for their reasons. Prince Bahman explained that they didn’t want to leave their sister, and that they were in the habit of doing nothing without talking it over among the three of them.
“Then ask her advice,” said the Sultan, “and come hunting with me again tomorrow, and give me your answer.”

The two princes went home, but the adventure had made so little impression on them that they forgot to mention it to their sister. The next morning they went hunting and met the Sultan at the same spot, and he asked what advice their sister had given. The young men looked at each other and blushed. At last Prince Bahman said, “Sire, we must throw ourselves on Your Highness’s mercy. Neither my brother nor I remembered it at all.”
“Then make sure you don’t forget today,” said the Sultan, “and bring me her reply tomorrow.”

But when the same thing happened a second time, they were afraid the Sultan might be angry at their carelessness. He took it kindly, though. He pulled three little golden balls out of his purse and handed them to Prince Bahman, saying, “Put these inside your shirt and you won’t forget a third time. When you take off your belt tonight, the noise they make as they fall will remind you of what I want.”
It all happened just as the Sultan had predicted. The two brothers arrived at their sister’s rooms just as she was getting into bed, and they told her their story.

Princess Parizade was very troubled by the news and made no secret of it. “Meeting the Sultan is a great honor for you,” she said, “and I dare say it will help you in future, but it puts me in an awkward position. I know it’s because of me that you refused the Sultan’s wishes, and I’m very grateful. But kings don’t like having their offers refused, and in time he would hold it against you, which would make me very unhappy. Ask the Talking Bird, who is wise and sees far ahead, and let me hear what he says.”
So the bird was sent for, and the matter was put before him.
“The princes must not refuse the Sultan’s offer under any circumstances,” he said, “and they should even invite him to come and see your house.”
“But bird,” protested the princess, “you know how much we love each other. Won’t all this spoil our friendship?”
“Not at all,” answered the bird. “It will bring you even closer.”
“Then the Sultan will have to see me,” said the princess.
The bird replied that he did need to see her, and that everything would turn out for the best.

The next morning the Sultan asked whether they had spoken to their sister and what advice she had given. Prince Bahman answered that they were ready to accept His Highness’s wishes, and that their sister had scolded them for hesitating. The Sultan accepted their apology very kindly. He told them he was sure they would be just as loyal to him, and he kept them at his side for the rest of the day, to the annoyance of the grand vizier and the rest of the court.
When the procession passed through the gates of the capital in this order, the crowds lining the streets kept their eyes on the two young men, who were strangers to everyone.
“Oh, if only the Sultan had sons like that!” they murmured. “They look so noble, and they’re about the age his own sons would have been!”

The Sultan ordered splendid rooms to be made ready for the two brothers, and he even insisted that they dine at his table. During dinner he steered the conversation to various branches of science and to history, which he loved especially. Whatever subject came up, he found that the young men’s opinions were always worth hearing. “If they were my own sons,” he told himself, “they couldn’t be better educated!” And out loud he praised them for their learning and their love of knowledge.

At the end of the evening the princes bowed to the ground again before the throne and asked permission to go home. Encouraged by the Sultan’s gracious words of farewell, Prince Bahman said, “Sire, may we be so bold as to ask whether you would do us and our sister the honor of resting for a few minutes at our house, the next time your hunt passes that way?”
“With the greatest pleasure,” answered the Sultan. “And since I’m impatient to meet the sister of such accomplished young men, you may expect me the day after tomorrow.”
The princess was eager, of course, to receive the Sultan properly, but she had no experience of court customs. So she ran to the Talking Bird and begged him to advise her on which dishes to serve.

“My dear mistress,” answered the bird, “your cooks are very good, and you can safely leave everything to them. Just make sure that a dish of cucumbers stuffed with pearl sauce is served with the first course.”

“Cucumbers stuffed with pearls!” cried the princess. “Bird, who ever heard of such a dish? The Sultan will expect a dinner he can eat, not one he can only look at! Besides, if I used every pearl I own, it wouldn’t be half enough.”

“Mistress,” said the bird, “do as I tell you and only good will come of it. As for the pearls, go at dawn tomorrow and dig at the foot of the first tree in the park, on the right-hand side. You’ll find as many as you need.”

The princess trusted the bird, who had generally proved right. Early the next morning she took the gardener with her and followed his directions carefully. After digging for a while, they came upon a golden box closed with little clasps.

The clasps were easy to undo, and the box turned out to be full of pearls. They weren’t very large, but they were well shaped and of a good color. The gardener stayed to fill in the hole he had dug under the tree, and the princess picked up the box and went back to the house.
The two princes had seen her leave, puzzled about why she was up at such an hour. Curious, they dressed quickly and caught their sister on her way back, carrying the box under her arm.
“What have you been doing?” they asked. “Did the gardener come to tell you he had found a treasure?”

“On the contrary,” answered the princess, “I’m the one who has found one.” She opened the box and showed her astonished brothers the pearls inside. Then, as they walked back to the palace, she told them about her talk with the bird and the advice it had given. All three tried to guess what such a strange instruction could mean, but in the end they had to admit it was beyond them and that they must simply obey without understanding.

The first thing the princess did on entering the palace was to send for the head cook and give her orders for the Sultan’s meal. When she had finished, she suddenly added, “Besides the dishes I’ve mentioned, there is one you must prepare especially for the Sultan, and no one but you is to touch it. It is a stuffed cucumber, and the stuffing is to be made from these pearls.”
The head cook had never in his whole career heard of such a dish, and he took a startled step backward.
“You think I’m mad,” said the princess, who saw what he was thinking. “But I know perfectly well what I’m doing. Go and do your best, and take the pearls with you.”

The next morning the princes set out for the forest, and the Sultan soon joined them. The hunt began and went on until midday, when the heat grew so fierce that they had to stop. Then, as planned, they turned their horses toward the palace. Prince Bahman stayed beside the Sultan, while Prince Perviz rode ahead to warn his sister that they were coming.

The moment His Highness entered the courtyard, the princess threw herself at his feet. He bent down and lifted her up, then gazed at her for some time. He was struck by her grace and beauty, and by the indefinable air of the court that seemed to surround this country girl. “They are all worthy of one another,” he said to himself, “and I’m not surprised that they value her opinions so highly. I must learn more about them.”
By now the princess had recovered from the awkwardness of their first meeting, and she began her speech of welcome.

“This is only a simple country house, sire,” she said, “fit for people like us, who live quietly. It can’t compare with the great mansions of the city, and certainly not with the smallest of the Sultan’s palaces.”
“I can’t quite agree with you,” he answered. “Even the little I’ve seen, I admire greatly, and I’ll hold back my judgment until you’ve shown me all of it.”

The princess then led him from room to room, and the Sultan inspected everything closely. “Do you call this a simple country house?” he said at last. “If every country house were like this, the towns would soon be empty. I’m no longer surprised that you don’t want to leave it. Let’s go out to the gardens, which I’m sure are every bit as beautiful as the rooms.”
A small door opened straight onto the garden, and the first thing the Sultan saw was the Golden Water.

“What beautifully colored water!” he exclaimed. “Where is the spring, and how do you make the fountain shoot up so high? I don’t believe there’s anything like it anywhere in the world.” He walked over to look at it, and when he had satisfied his curiosity, the princess led him toward the Singing Tree.

As they came closer, the Sultan was startled by the sound of strange voices, though he could see no one. “Where have you hidden your musicians?” he asked the princess. “Are they up in the air, or under the ground? Surely the owners of such lovely voices shouldn’t hide themselves!”
“Sire,” answered the princess, “all the voices come from the tree directly in front of us. If you will be so kind as to take a few steps closer, you will hear them more clearly.”
The Sultan did as she said, and he was so lost in delight at what he heard that he stood in silence for some time.

“Madam, tell me, please,” he said at last, “how did this marvelous tree end up in your garden? It must have come from far away, because I love curiosities of every kind and I would surely have heard of it otherwise. What is it called?”

“It has only one name, sire,” she answered. “It is called the Singing Tree, and it does not come from this country. Its story is bound up with the stories of the Golden Water and the Talking Bird, which you have not seen yet. If your Highness wishes, I will tell you the whole tale once you have rested from your journey.”
“Madam,” he replied, “you show me so many wonders that I cannot possibly feel tired. Let us go and look at the Golden Water once more, and then I am longing to see the Talking Bird.”

The Sultan could barely pull himself away from the Golden Water, which baffled him more and more. “You tell me,” he said to the princess, “that this water comes from no spring and is not carried in by pipes. All I can make out is that neither the water nor the Singing Tree belongs to this country.”

“That is so, sire,” the princess answered. “And if you look closely at the basin, you will see it is all in one piece, so the water cannot have been piped into it. What is more astonishing is that I poured only a small flask of it into the basin, and it grew to the amount you see now.”
“Very well, I will look at it no more today,” said the Sultan. “Take me to the Talking Bird.”
As they came near the house, the Sultan saw a huge crowd of birds whose voices filled the air, and he asked why there were so many more here than anywhere else in the garden.

“Sire,” the princess answered, “do you see the cage hanging in one of the windows of the saloon? That is the Talking Bird. You can hear his voice above all the others, even above the nightingale’s. The birds gather in this spot to add their songs to his.”
The Sultan stepped in through the window, but the bird paid him no attention and went on singing as before.
“My slave,” said the princess, “this is the Sultan. Give him a fine welcome.”
At once the bird stopped singing, and every other bird fell silent as well.
“Welcome to the Sultan,” he said. “I wish him a long life and every happiness.”
“Thank you, good bird,” the Sultan answered, sitting down before the meal, which was laid out on a table beside the window. “I am delighted to see in you the Sultan and King of the Birds.”

The Sultan saw that his favorite dish, stuffed cucumber, had been set in front of him. He helped himself, and was amazed to find that the stuffing was made of pearls. “Now that is something new!” he cried. “But I cannot see the point of it. Nobody can eat pearls!”

“Sire,” the bird replied, before either the princes or the princess could speak, “surely your Highness cannot be so surprised to see a cucumber stuffed with pearls, when you had no trouble believing that the Sultana had given you a dog, a cat and a log of wood instead of children.”
“I believed it,” the Sultan answered, “because the women who waited on her told me so.”

“Those women, sire,” said the bird, “were the Sultana’s own sisters. They were eaten up with jealousy over the honor you had shown her, and they made up this story to take their revenge. Have them questioned and they will confess their crime. These are your children. The intendant of your gardens saved them from death and raised them as though they were his own.”

The truth struck the Sultan in an instant. “Bird,” he cried, “my heart tells me that what you say is true. My children,” he went on, “let me hold you, and hold each other too, not only as brothers and sister, but as people who carry the royal blood of Persia, which could run in no nobler veins.”

When the first rush of feeling had passed, the Sultan hurried to finish his meal. Then he turned to his children and said: “Today you have come to know your father. Tomorrow I will bring you the Sultana, your mother. Be ready to receive her.”

Then the Sultan mounted his horse and rode swiftly back to the capital. Without losing a moment he summoned the grand vizier and ordered him to arrest the Sultana’s sisters and question them that same day. It was done. They were set face to face, found guilty, and put to death in less than an hour.

Yet the Sultan would not wait for word that his orders were done. With his entire court following, he walked to the door of the great mosque, and there he took the Sultana by the hand and drew her out of the cramped prison where she had spent so many years. Tears stood in his eyes as he embraced her. “Madam,” he cried, “I am here to ask your forgiveness for the injustice I did you, and to undo it as far as I can. I have begun by punishing the people behind this abominable crime, and I hope you will pardon me once you meet our children, the most charming and accomplished young people in the world. Come with me. Take back your rank and every honor that belongs to you.”
These words were spoken before an enormous crowd, who had gathered from every direction at the first hint of what was happening, and within seconds the news had passed from mouth to mouth.

Early the next day the Sultan and the Sultana, dressed in robes of state with the whole court behind them, set out for their children’s country house. There the Sultan presented the children to the Sultana one by one, and for a while there was nothing but embraces, tears and tender words. Then they ate the magnificent dinner that had been prepared for them, and when they had all refreshed themselves they went into the garden, where the Sultan showed his wife the Golden Water and the Singing Tree. The Talking Bird she had already met.

In the evening they rode back to the capital together, with the princes on either side of their father and the princess beside her mother. Long before they reached the gates, people lined the road and the air rang with shouts of welcome. Mingled with them were the songs of the Talking Bird, sitting in his cage on the princess’s lap, and of the birds that followed him.
And so they came back to their father’s palace.
